title: Best Whiskey for No Hangover: Bourbon vs Irish vs Scotch
excerpt: Which whiskey is easiest on your next morning? How bourbon, Irish whiskey, and Scotch compare on congeners, why age and char don't protect you, and how to buy and drink smarter.
metaDescription: Which whiskey gives the mildest hangover? Bourbon vs Irish vs Scotch congeners, age and char myths, and what to look for when you buy a bottle.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no whiskey that gives you no hangover. Whiskey is one of the higher-congener spirits, which means it carries more of the extra flavor compounds that are linked to worse mornings, and the alcohol itself does most of the damage anyway. But whiskey is a huge category, and the bottle does matter a little. The gentler picks tend to be **younger, lighter whiskeys at a normal bottling strength, without added flavors or sweeteners**. The rougher picks tend to be **heavily aged, cask-strength, flavored, or sweetened whiskeys**, especially when you drink them fast.

**The quick rules:** don't assume older or more expensive means cleaner, because more years in oak usually means more congeners, not fewer. Skip honey, cinnamon, and other flavored whiskeys. Choose standard strength (around 40% to 46% ABV) over cask strength unless you add water. Drink it with water, over ice, or as a tall highball rather than as shots. Keep the number of drinks modest, eat first, and have a glass of water between rounds.

> **A quick note on safety.** This guide is about choosing whiskey and drinking it sensibly. It isn't medical advice. **See a doctor or get emergency care if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has cold or bluish skin, or has a seizure. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover, so call 911 (in the US) and don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." If you regularly get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop drinking, talk to a doctor, because that can be a sign your body has become dependent on alcohol. And if you take any regular medication, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether alcohol is safe with it.

## Why Whiskey Hangovers Feel Worse: Congeners in Plain Words

Every alcoholic drink contains ethanol, the alcohol that gets you drunk. Most also contain smaller amounts of other compounds called **congeners**. These are by-products of fermentation, distillation, and aging. They give drinks much of their flavor, smell, and color. They include things like methanol, fusel alcohols (heavier alcohols with an oily, solvent-like note), aldehydes, esters, and compounds pulled out of the wooden barrel such as tannins and vanillin. We cover them in detail in our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

The general pattern in the research is that **darker drinks carry more congeners than clear ones**, and drinks high in congeners tend to produce worse hangovers at the same amount of alcohol. Whiskey sits near the top of that list, along with brandy, dark rum, and red wine. Vodka and gin sit near the bottom.

The clearest human evidence comes from a controlled study published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010 by Damaris Rohsenow and colleagues. Healthy young adults drank either bourbon or vodka until they reached the same fairly high breath-alcohol level, and the researchers measured how they felt the next morning. The bourbon drinkers reported **worse hangovers** than the vodka drinkers. Interestingly, next-day performance on tasks like attention and reaction time was impaired by both drinks about equally. So the congeners seemed to make people feel worse, while the alcohol itself did most of the damage to how well they functioned.

An older British study from the 1970s, which compared several drinks, also found that brandy and darker spirits like whisky tended to produce worse hangovers than vodka. The study was small and dated, but it lines up with the later research.

Two caveats are worth keeping in mind:

- **The difference is real but modest.** People in the vodka group were still hungover. Switching from whiskey to vodka shaves off some of the misery, it doesn't remove it.
- **Nobody has tested whiskey styles against each other.** We could not find good controlled studies comparing bourbon with Scotch, Irish whiskey, or rye for hangovers. Everything below about styles is based on how they are made and what that tends to mean for congener levels, not on direct head-to-head trials.

For a deeper look at why whiskey mornings hit the way they do, see our guide to the [whiskey hangover](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).

## What Makes One Whiskey Different From Another

Before comparing styles, it helps to know the four things that most affect how many congeners end up in the glass.

**1. How it's distilled.** Distillation separates alcohol from the fermented mash. A tall column still run to a high strength strips out more congeners and gives a lighter spirit. A traditional copper pot still, run to a lower strength, keeps more of the heavier flavor compounds. Distillers also "cut" the run, setting aside the first part (the heads, rich in volatile compounds) and the last part (the tails, rich in heavier fusel oils). How tightly they cut affects how clean the new spirit is.

**2. How many times it's distilled.** Extra distillation generally gives a lighter spirit. That's one reason many Irish whiskeys, which are often triple distilled, taste softer than many Scotches, which are usually distilled twice.

**3. The barrel.** Most of whiskey's color and a large share of its flavor come from the oak. New, heavily charred barrels (the rule for bourbon) give up a lot of wood compounds quickly. Used barrels, such as ex-bourbon or ex-sherry casks (the norm for Scotch and Irish), give up less per year but are often used for longer.

**4. Time.** The longer whiskey sits in wood, the more wood-derived compounds it picks up, and some harsh compounds also react and change over time. Age makes whiskey smoother to taste, but that smoothness doesn't mean fewer congeners. In general, older means more.

Then there's what gets added after aging: water to bring it down to bottling strength, and in some styles, caramel coloring or flavoring. We'll come back to that.

## Bourbon vs Irish vs Scotch vs Rye: How the Styles Compare

Here's a style-by-style look. Treat it as a guide to likely congener levels and drinking habits, not a guarantee about your hangover.

### Bourbon

US rules require bourbon to be made from at least 51% corn, aged in **new charred oak containers**, and bottled at no less than 80 proof (40% ABV). It can't contain added coloring or flavoring. That no-additives rule is a genuine plus. You know exactly what's in the bottle: grain spirit, water, and what the barrel gave it.

The flip side is the new charred oak. It's very active, so bourbon picks up a lot of color and wood compounds even in a few years. Bourbon is the spirit that was tested in the bourbon-versus-vodka study above, and it came out worse. Many popular bourbons are also bottled at higher strengths, such as 100 proof for bottled-in-bond, or as "barrel proof" at 55% ABV or more.

**Gentler bourbon choices:** a younger straight bourbon at around 40% to 45% ABV. Wheated bourbons (with wheat instead of rye as the secondary grain) taste softer, but we know of no evidence they're easier on you the next morning.

**Rougher bourbon choices:** barrel-proof bottles drunk neat, very old "extra-aged" bourbons, and any bourbon taken as fast shots.

### Irish Whiskey

Irish whiskey must be aged at least three years in wooden casks in Ireland. Many of the best-known brands are triple distilled and blended with lighter grain whiskey, which gives a smooth, light style. Caramel coloring is allowed, and some brands use it to keep the color consistent.

Of the major whiskey styles, a standard **Irish blend is probably among the lighter options** in terms of congeners. That's a reasonable inference from how it's made, not something a study has measured for hangovers. Single pot still Irish whiskey, made from a mix of malted and unmalted barley in pot stills, is richer and heavier, so it doesn't share that advantage to the same degree.

### Scotch

Scotch must be made in Scotland and aged at least three years in oak casks. Single malts are made only from malted barley, usually in copper pot stills, and are usually distilled twice. Blended Scotch mixes malt whisky with lighter grain whisky made in column stills, so most blends are lighter than most single malts. Caramel coloring (labeled E150a in some markets) is allowed, though many single malts now say "natural color" or "no added coloring" on the label.

**Peated Scotch**, the smoky style from places like Islay, gets its smoke from drying the barley over peat fires. That adds compounds called phenols. There's no good evidence that peat itself makes hangovers worse, but heavily peated whiskies are full-flavored, high-congener drinks, and they are often bottled at higher strengths.

**Gentler Scotch choices:** a younger blend or a lighter, unpeated single malt at standard strength. **Rougher choices:** old, sherry-cask single malts, heavily peated cask-strength bottles, and anything drunk quickly.

### Rye

American rye whiskey follows rules similar to bourbon's: at least 51% rye, aged in new charred oak, with no additives allowed. It has a spicier, drier taste. In congener terms, it's in the same territory as bourbon. There's no reason to expect it to be gentler or worse.

### Canadian, Tennessee, and Japanese Whisky

- **Canadian whisky** is often light-bodied and blended, much of it made with column stills. Canadian rules allow a small proportion of other flavorings, so some bottles contain more than grain, water, and wood. Lighter style, but check the label for flavored versions.
- **Tennessee whiskey** is made much like bourbon, but most of it is filtered through sugar maple charcoal before aging (the "Lincoln County Process"). Fans say this makes it smoother. We know of no good evidence that it makes hangovers milder.
- **Japanese whisky** varies a lot, from light, delicate blends to rich single malts. Historically, some products labeled Japanese whisky contained imported spirit. Industry labeling standards introduced in 2021 have tightened that, but the style of the bottle still matters more than the country.

### The short version by style

| Style | Typical congener profile | Gentler pick within the style |
|---|---|---|
| Irish blend | Lighter (often triple distilled, blended with grain whiskey) | Standard blend at 40% ABV |
| Blended Scotch | Lighter to medium | Younger blend, unpeated |
| Canadian | Lighter (often column-distilled blends) | Unflavored blend |
| Single malt Scotch | Medium to heavy | Younger, unpeated, standard strength |
| Bourbon / rye | Medium to heavy (new charred oak) | Younger straight bourbon at 40-45% ABV |
| Cask-strength anything | Heavy, plus more alcohol per sip | Add water, pour smaller |

## Whiskey Myths That Don't Hold Up

**"Older whiskey is cleaner."** It's smoother to taste, but it has spent more time picking up compounds from the wood. If anything, older whiskey tends to carry more congeners. There's no good evidence that a 21-year-old gives you a milder hangover than a 6-year-old.

**"Expensive whiskey won't give you a hangover."** Price mostly tracks age, rarity, and branding. Better whiskey may have fewer harsh off-notes, but no bottle cancels out the alcohol. People also tend to drink special bottles neat, which means more alcohol per sip.

**"The char is a filter, so it cleans the whiskey."** Charring the inside of a barrel does help strip out some harsh sulfur compounds and changes the flavor, and charcoal filtering (as in Tennessee whiskey) removes some compounds before aging. But the same charred oak then adds a lot of new wood compounds over the years. The net effect is a darker, richer spirit, not a lighter one. There's no good evidence that char or charcoal filtering reduces hangovers.

**"Single malt is purer than a blend."** "Single malt" means all the whisky comes from one distillery and is made from malted barley. It doesn't mean fewer congeners. Most blends include lighter grain whisky, so they are often lower in congeners than a single malt.

**"Peat causes headaches."** Plenty of people say smoky whisky hits them harder, and some may be sensitive to it. But we know of no good evidence that peat itself causes hangovers. It's more likely about strength, the amount, and the fact that peated whiskies are full-flavored, heavy drinks.

**"Whiskey is the healthiest spirit."** You'll see claims online about whiskey's antioxidants, such as ellagic acid from the oak. The amounts in a normal drink are small, and any possible benefit is outweighed by the alcohol. Don't pick whiskey for your health.

**"Switching drinks causes hangovers."** Mixing whiskey with beer or wine doesn't harm you through some special chemistry. It's the total amount that counts. Our article on [the beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) covers the research.

## How to Buy a Whiskey That's Easier on You

If you're choosing a bottle with the next morning in mind, here's a practical checklist.

1. **Check the strength.** Look for 40% to 46% ABV. Cask-strength and barrel-proof bottles (often 55% to 65% ABV) put a lot more alcohol into each pour. If you love them, add water and pour less.
2. **Skip flavored whiskeys.** Honey, cinnamon, apple, and similar "whiskey" products are often lower in alcohol but are sweetened and flavored, which makes them easy to drink fast and in large amounts. Many are technically "liqueurs" or "spirit drinks."
3. **Favor younger and lighter.** A younger straight bourbon, an Irish blend, a blended Scotch, or a light unpeated malt is likely lower in congeners than an old, heavily oaked bottle.
4. **Read the coloring line.** For Scotch and Irish whiskey, "natural color" or "no added coloring" tells you nothing extra went in. For bourbon and American rye, no coloring is allowed anyway. Caramel coloring is used in tiny amounts and there's no good evidence it worsens hangovers, but a clean label is a decent sign the producer isn't dressing the whiskey up.
5. **Don't pay for a hangover cure.** Spend more if you enjoy the flavor, not because you expect a better morning.
6. **Consider whether whiskey is the right drink tonight.** If you know you'll have several drinks, a clear spirit is likely to be a little gentler. See our picks for the [best vodka for no hangover](/never-hungover/best-vodka-for-no-hangover) and the [best tequila for no hangover](/never-hungover/best-tequila-for-no-hangover), or our full [least-hangover alcohol ranking](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).

## How You Drink It Matters More Than Which Bottle

Picking a lighter whiskey helps a little. How you drink it helps a lot more.

**Count standard drinks.** In the US, one standard drink is 1.5 ounces (about 44 ml) of 40% ABV whiskey. A generous home pour, a double at a bar, or a cask-strength dram can easily be two standard drinks or more. The amount of alcohol is the biggest single driver of how you'll feel tomorrow.

**Slow down.** Sipping whiskey is one of its genuine advantages. A neat pour that lasts half an hour is far gentler than a round of shots. Your liver can only clear roughly one standard drink an hour, so pacing keeps your blood alcohol lower.

**Add water and ice.** A splash of water opens up the flavor, and a highball (whiskey with lots of ice and soda water) stretches one drink over a longer time. Both make it easier to drink less.

**Watch sugary mixers.** Whiskey and cola, whiskey sours made with bottled sour mix, and sweet punches go down fast. Caffeinated mixers and energy drinks can also mask how drunk you feel, which makes it easier to overdo it.

**Eat before and during.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood. A proper meal before you start drinking is one of the simplest ways to soften the next day.

**Drink water between rounds.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and dehydration adds to a headache and dry mouth. Water won't prevent a hangover by itself, but it helps, and it slows your pace. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains when an electrolyte drink is worth it.

**Protect your sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep in the second half of the night, and poor sleep makes a hangover worse. Stopping a couple of hours before bed helps.

For a fuller plan, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people add a supplement to their night out. The most-discussed one is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the brain's response to alcohol. Most of that research is in animals and lab settings, with very limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people, and it doesn't change how much alcohol you take in. It's an optional extra, not a replacement for choosing a lighter whiskey and drinking less of it.

If you'd like to try it, people commonly choose [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) as a budget option or [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly. If you take any medication, check with a pharmacist before adding a supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- **No whiskey gives you no hangover.** The amount of alcohol is the main cause, and whiskey is a higher-congener spirit to begin with.
- **Lighter and younger beats older and heavier.** Irish blends, blended Scotch, and younger straight bourbons are likely gentler than old, heavily oaked, or cask-strength bottles.
- **Age, price, and char aren't hangover protection.** Older whiskey usually has more congeners, not fewer.
- **Skip flavored whiskeys and sugary, fast-drinking mixers.**
- **Drink slowly, add water, eat, and count your pours.** That does more for tomorrow than any bottle can.

Not set on whiskey? Our guide to the [best liquor for no hangover](/never-hungover/best-liquor-for-no-hangover) ranks every major spirit, from vodka and gin to rum and brandy.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best whiskey for no hangover?**

No whiskey prevents a hangover, because the alcohol itself is the main cause. If you want the best odds, choose a younger, lighter whiskey over a heavily aged or cask-strength one, prefer a straight bourbon or a single malt that states it has no added coloring, skip flavored and honey whiskeys, and drink it with plenty of water or soda. Then keep the number of drinks modest, sip slowly, and eat beforehand. How much you drink matters far more than which bottle you pick.

**Is bourbon, Irish whiskey, or Scotch better for hangovers?**

There is no good evidence from controlled studies that compares bourbon, Irish whiskey, and Scotch head to head for hangovers. All three are dark, wood-aged spirits with plenty of congeners (the flavor by-products of fermentation and aging). Lighter, younger Irish blends are often lower in congeners than an old, heavily oaked bourbon or a peaty Scotch, so they may be a little gentler for some people, but the difference is small compared with the effect of how much you drink.

**Does more expensive or older whiskey give you less of a hangover?**

Not reliably. Older whiskey has spent more time in oak, which usually means more wood-derived congeners, not fewer. Price mostly reflects age, rarity, and branding. A pricey 18-year-old can be just as rough the next morning as a mid-priced bottle, and possibly rougher. Better quality can mean fewer harsh off-notes, but it does not cancel out the alcohol.

**Is whiskey worse for hangovers than vodka?**

On average, probably a little. In a well-known controlled study, people who drank bourbon to the same breath-alcohol level as people who drank vodka reported somewhat worse hangovers the next day, and bourbon contains far more congeners than vodka. But the gap was modest, and the vodka drinkers were hungover too. Drinking less whiskey slowly will usually leave you better off than drinking a lot of vodka quickly.

**Do whiskey and Coke or other mixers make hangovers worse?**

Sugary mixers can make it easier to drink more, and faster, and they add sugar and sometimes caffeine, which can mask how drunk you feel. Some small studies suggest diet mixers may raise blood alcohol a bit faster than sugary ones, so neither is a free pass. The simplest option is whiskey with water or soda water, or a highball with plenty of ice and a lot of soda, which slows you down.

**Can DHM help with a whiskey hangover?**

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the brain's response to alcohol, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. Some people take it with drinks, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people, and it does not change how much alcohol reaches your blood. It is an optional extra on top of drinking less and drinking slower, not a replacement for either.
